mcqs.question: What does "baseline fluency" with a remote whiteboard tool actually require?
options: Mastery of every feature the tool offers
Memorizing the tool's keyboard shortcut list in full
Knowing the five or six actions you'll use constantly — box, labeled arrow, text, undo, pan/zoom — well enough that they're automatic
Choosing your own whiteboard tool ahead of the interview
mcqs.explanation: A small set of frequently-used actions being automatic is what matters — full feature mastery or a memorized shortcut list isn't necessary, and candidates rarely get to choose the tool themselves.

mcqs.question: Why is shrinking text and boxes to fit more onto a remote whiteboard canvas a worse habit than starting a labeled second canvas?
options: Shrinking text is technically impossible in most whiteboard tools
Second canvases are required by every interview process
Shrinking is only a problem if the interviewer is using a phone
Shrunk-down elements become genuinely hard to read at typical video-call resolution, unlike a clearly separated second area
mcqs.explanation: Video-call resolution makes small, cramped text disproportionately harder to read remotely than it would be on a physical board — a labeled second canvas preserves legibility instead. It's not a tool limitation, isn't a formal requirement, and isn't specific to phone viewers.

mcqs.question: What should a candidate do first when their screen or whiteboard tool freezes mid-interview?
options: Say what's happening out loud immediately, and keep describing the design verbally if the visual can't be fixed quickly
Stay silent while troubleshooting to avoid distracting the interviewer
End the call and ask to reschedule the interview
Wait for the interviewer to notice and ask what's wrong
mcqs.explanation: Naming the problem immediately and continuing verbally keeps the interview progressing and shows composure — most interviewers have seen this before and judge the response, not the failure itself. Going silent or waiting to be asked wastes time, and rescheduling is a drastic overreaction to a recoverable glitch.

mcqs.question: Why does fumbling with an unfamiliar whiteboard tool for the first several minutes of a remote interview cost more than it might seem?
options: It has no real cost as long as the final design is correct
It eats directly into the same fixed 45 minutes everyone gets, and disrupts narration right when a strong first impression matters most
It only matters if the interviewer explicitly comments on it
Tool fluency is evaluated as a separate, formal scoring category
mcqs.explanation: Time lost to tool fumbling is time subtracted from the same fixed interview length, and it visibly disrupts the opening minutes — the cost is real regardless of whether the interviewer comments on it or whether tool skill is formally scored.
